rgb: This indoor floor-work area is seen from directly above through the kneeling camera wearer’s viewpoint. Dark wood-grain laminate boards partly cover a dark, speckled underlayment, with white walls and a doorway bordering the space. The wearer’s torso, knees, and extended arms occupy the lower foreground; both hands rest on the floor approximately 0.5 to 0.7 metres below the head-mounted camera and are separated by about 0.3 to 0.5 metres. During the first three frames, the wearer looks straight toward a white wall corner around 0.6 to 0.8 metres ahead. A metal putty knife sits on the planks between the hands and slightly beyond them, within arm’s reach and roughly 0.6 metres from the camera. From frames 2 through 5, the wearer turns clockwise by about 90 degrees and moves backward and to the right onto the exposed underlayment, bringing both hands nearer the knees along the uncovered edges of the planks. In frame 5, the putty knife is farther left at about 0.8 metres, while a red-and-black tool and a hand tool lie on the underlayment at the far right, approximately 0.8 to 1.0 metre away. Part of another person’s hand and lower leg also enters at the upper-right edge, roughly 1.0 to 1.2 metres in front of the wearer. Nearly all of that person, the higher portions of the walls, and the rest of the room fall outside the downward-facing view, and the wearer’s torso and arms obscure part of the floor immediately underneath.
depth: The depth visualization presents a downward-looking egocentric perspective of a floor corner, enclosed by walls at the upper left and a cabinet at the lower left, 0.4–0.8 m away. In the foreground, the wearer’s torso, knees, and extended arms span depths of 0.1–0.7 m, with the hands placed on floorboards and subfloor at 0.7–1.1 m, all within reaching distance. A metal scraper is also reachable at 0.6–0.9 m and sits about 0.2–0.4 m between the hands. From frames 1 through 3, the wearer moves slightly rightward and draws both hands in toward the torso. In frame 4, they rotate approximately 90 degrees counter-clockwise, causing the bright white chest and flexed knees, at 0.1–0.4 m, to dominate the lower foreground. The wearer then leans higher in frame 5, when another person’s hand and leg become visible along the top-right boundary at about 1.1 m, directed toward the floor rather than looking at the wearer. The wearer’s torso, arms, and knees block the planks underneath, while their head and nearly the entire second person remain beyond the image borders. Relative to RGB by itself, the depth changes distinctly separate the raised vertical wall surfaces and the wearer’s elevated knees and limbs from the level floor below, while only faintly revealing the scraper’s height in frame 3. Still, the map becomes unreliable when frame-by-frame auto-scaling reverses the apparent brightness ordering: the floor appears much darker and more distant in frame 2 than in frame 1 even though its distance is comparable. It also fails in frame 5, where the scraper and the small right-side tools disappear entirely within the dark floor gradient.
segmentation: Only areas assigned to the ‘person’ category are marked by the segmentation output, including foreground regions at 0.1–0.7 m and an area at the upper-right edge of frame 5 at approximately 1.1 m. The walls, cabinet, wooden boards, subfloor, and hand tools are all left completely black and unlabeled, even though they lie within the wearer’s 0.7 m reaching range. In frames 1–3, the wearer’s left arm appears on the left at 0.3–0.7 m, the right arm appears on the right at 0.3–0.7 m and about 0.4 m from the left arm, and the lower torso and knees occupy the bottom center at 0.1–0.5 m. These body regions move downward and right before turning counter-clockwise in frame 4, when the torso and knees spread over the bottom foreground and hide some of the floor beneath them. As the wearer leans back slightly in frame 5, a yellow/green mask along the top-right border identifies the newly visible hand and leg of a second person. That person is about 1.1 m away and roughly 0.6 m in front of the wearer’s right hand, remains mostly beyond the upper frame boundary, and is oriented toward the floor rather than toward the camera wearer. This entrance is less immediately noticeable against the wood and subfloor in RGB alone. Nevertheless, the instance segmentation is very unreliable: it divides the camera wearer’s one body into two or three different ‘person’ instances colored cyan, pink, and brown, and those colors change between frames. In frame 4, it also incorrectly joins a broad section of wooden flooring between the arms to the brown ‘person’ region.
pose: Against a fully black background, the pose output displays only magenta 2D hand skeletons for the camera wearer’s left and right hands, positioned around 0.5–0.7 m from the camera and 0.25–0.5 m from one another. It excludes every part of the scene’s geometry, all tools on the floor, and every yellow body skeleton. Throughout frames 1–3, the two hands remain palm-down and within reaching distance on the floorboards, moving from the upper-left/central area toward the lower center while the wearer backs up and turns slightly right in relation to the corner. In frame 4, the wearer rotates counter-clockwise and bends forward, extending both hands toward the image’s upper boundary at approximately 0.7 m away. The hands widen to around 0.5 m apart and lie on opposite sides of the knees. By frame 5, they pull back into the lower half of the frame, approximately 0.6 m from the camera and about 0.25 m apart, resting across the planks and subfloor. Compared with RGB alone, this representation reveals the precise finger positions, thumb-to-index separation, and wrist alignment of both wearer hands much more clearly. Its wider spatial interpretation is unreliable, however, because it does not identify the wearer’s visible arms, shoulders, or knees, which are partly self-occluded and cut off by the lower image boundary. It also entirely overlooks the second person’s visible hand at the top-right border in frame 5, approximately 1.1 m away and within reaching distance of the tools and upper floorboards.
